lead: A context-free grammar is a set of rewriting rules plus a start symbol. Rewrite the start symbol until no symbol can be rewritten; the ordinary letters left form a string of the language. This idea explains why programming languages nest brackets, blocks and expressions without limit. Compilers build parse trees from such grammars, and the grammar yacc, bison and ANTLR read is the same object, written in BNF or EBNF with declarations and actions added.
prereq: You need Unit 1: alphabets, strings, languages and the Kleene star, from alphabets, strings and formal languages.

sections.h3: A grammar is a four-part rewriting machine

blocks.text: A context-free grammar produces strings by rewriting. Start with one symbol, replace it using a rule, and keep replacing until only ordinary letters remain. Those letters form a string of the grammar's language.

blocks.where: G is the grammar; V is the finite set of variables (nonterminals), written in capitals such as S, A, B; T is the finite set of terminals, the letters of final strings, written in lowercase such as a, b, or as words such as id; P is the finite set of productions; S is the start symbol, and S ∈ V. V and T are finite, nonempty and disjoint.

blocks.text: The union V ∪ T is the alphabet of the grammar. Every production has one variable on the left and any string of variables and terminals on the right.
A → α, with A ∈ V and α ∈ (V ∪ T)*
blocks.where: A is the single variable being replaced; α (alpha) is the replacement string, possibly empty; (V ∪ T)* means any finite sequence of variables and terminals, including the empty sequence.

blocks.text: The name context-free describes the left side. A rule replaces A wherever A appears. Nothing is tested about symbols beside A. A context-sensitive rule such as aAb → aXb is not allowed in a CFG, because it demands that A be between a and b.

Why the model exists: nesting. A finite automaton has a fixed number of states, so it cannot compare a count on the left with a count on the right. The pair of rules S → aSb | ε adds one a at the front and one b at the back per step, and S → ε ends with the counts equal. Nested brackets, nested if-else chains and nested arithmetic need exactly this power.

Two shorthand forms keep grammars short. The bar | separates alternatives, so S → aSb | ε stands for two productions. The symbol ε (epsilon) is the empty string, of length zero. Round brackets group symbols on a right side: with B → b | c, the rule A → a(B)c is shorthand for A → abc | acc.

items: Equal a's then b's: S → aSb | ε gives {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}. In order of length: ε, ab, aabb, aaabbb.

Balanced round brackets: S → (S)S | ε gives every bracket string that closes properly, such as ()() and (()). Here ( and ) are terminals of the language, not the grouping shorthand. The string )( is not generated.
Palindromes over {a, b}: S → aSa | bSb | a | b | ε gives strings that read the same both ways, such as abba and baab.
Arithmetic expressions: E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → (E) | id. Here id is a number or variable name. The three levels force × to bind tighter than +, and F reaches the brackets.
if-else in C: S → if (C) S | if (C) S else S | other. C is a condition and other is any simple statement. This grammar is ambiguous for the dangling else, as 3.3 shows.

blocks.text: A derivation is the written record of rewriting. Write u ⇒ v when one step turns string u into string v: one variable inside u is replaced by the right side of one of its productions. Write u ⇒* v for zero or more such steps; the star is the Kleene star applied to the arrow.

blocks.where: L(G) is the language generated by G; w ranges over strings of terminals only; S ⇒* w means the start symbol reaches w in finitely many steps.

items: Pick any variable and any production for it; replace that one occurrence.
The remaining terminal string belongs to L(G).

blocks.text: Which variable you expand, and in what order, does not change the set of strings you can reach. Two orders of the same expansion give two derivations of the same string, and drawn as a tree they are the same tree. Trees are the subject of 3.2.

Only a few universities teach the phrase "type 2 grammar" in the first course: in the Chomsky hierarchy a type 2 grammar is exactly a context-free grammar (see 3.9). BNF in compiler books is the same object with ::= instead of → and angle brackets around variables.

figure.caption: Each rewriting step replaces the one variable S by a rule’s right side; after three steps no variable is left and aabb is in L(G). Each use of S → aSb adds a matching a and b, so the strings of length at most 6 are ε, ab, aabb and aaabbb.

spec.aria: A derivation S, aSb, aaSbb, aabb with each arrow labelled by the rule used, then the four strings ε, ab, aabb, aaabbb with their lengths 0, 2, 4 and 6.

examples.question: Let G = ({S}, {a, b}, P, S) with P: S → aSb | ε. (i) Derive aabb with every intermediate string. (ii) List every string of L(G) of length at most 6, and give the count.
steps: The bar gives S → aSb and S → ε.
Step 2: aSb ⇒ aaSbb by applying S → aSb to the middle S.
Step 3: aaSbb ⇒ aabb by S → ε. No variable remains, so aabb ∈ L(G).
The rule shape forces aⁿbⁿ: each aSb step adds one a in front and one b at the back. Hence L(G) = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}.
Strings by n: ε (n = 0, length 0), ab (n = 1, length 2), aabb (n = 2, length 4), aaabbb (n = 3, length 6). The next, aaaabbbb, has length 8.
Count of strings of length at most 6 = 4.
examples.answer: S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aabb takes 3 steps; L(G) = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} has exactly 4 strings of length at most 6: ε, ab, aabb and aaabbb. In the printed output, the k = 0 line is the empty string shown with quotes.
examples.check:
w = 'aabb'
cur, deriv = 'S', ['S']
for _ in range(2):
    cur = cur.replace('S', 'aSb', 1)
    deriv.append(cur)
cur = cur.replace('S', '', 1)
deriv.append(cur)
assert deriv[-1] == w
na, nb = w.count('a'), w.count('b')
steps = len(deriv) - 1
limit = 6
short = ['a' * k + 'b' * k for k in range(limit + 1)
         if len('a' * k + 'b' * k) <= limit]
print(na)
print(nb)
print(steps)
print(len(short))

for k in range(4):
    print('k = ' + str(k) + ': ' + repr('a' * k + 'b' * k))

traps: The grammar is not the language. {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} is generated by S → ab | aSb as well as by S → aSb | ε with the ε case unused; to get all of {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} from a different rule list, use S → A, A → aAb | ε. The bar is shorthand for two productions, never a character of the generated string.
ε is a string, not a letter inside a derivation. S → ε erases S; it does not leave ε in the string. L(G) contains ε exactly when S ⇒* ε.
A production must be context-free: the left side is exactly one variable. Writing aS → ab or SA → aA is not allowed, and examiners deduct marks for it without comment.
Each step replaces exactly one occurrence of one variable. Replacing every S at once, or assuming two expansion orders give two different parse trees, is wrong.
L(G) holds terminal strings only. A string with a variable still in it is an intermediate sentential form, not a word of the language.

quiz.q: Define a context-free grammar as a 4-tuple and state which set the start symbol belongs to.
quiz.a: G = (V, T, P, S), with V variables, T terminals, P productions of the form A → α where A ∈ V and α ∈ (V ∪ T)*. The start symbol S is an element of V.

quiz.q: Why is the model called context-free? What is it free of?
quiz.a: Every left side is a single variable, so the rule applies wherever that variable occurs. No context of neighbouring symbols is ever tested.

quiz.q: Give L(G) for the grammar S → aSbb | ε.
quiz.a: Each step adds one a and two b's, so L(G) = {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 0} = {ε, abb, aabbbb, aaabbbbbb, ...}.

quiz.q: Show a derivation of baab from S → aSa | bSb | ε, counting the steps.
quiz.a: S ⇒ bSb ⇒ baSab ⇒ baab. Three steps; the last applies S → ε inside the pair a…a.

quiz.q: G1: S → aSb | ε and G2: S → ab | aSb. Do these grammars generate the same language? Justify.
quiz.a: G1 gives {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}, including ε. G2 gives {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} and can never produce ε. L(G1) ≠ L(G2) because ε ∈ L(G1) but ε ∉ L(G2), so the two grammars are not equivalent.

quiz.q: The grammar S → SS | a generates aaa. Give two different derivations and say what this means for the grammar.
quiz.a: First: S ⇒ SS ⇒ aS ⇒ aSS ⇒ aaS ⇒ aaa. Second: S ⇒ SS ⇒ Sa ⇒ SSa ⇒ aSa ⇒ aaa. Two different parse trees for one string make the grammar ambiguous; 3.3 takes this up.

quiz.q: Can a string of L(G) contain a variable? Why?
quiz.a: No. L(G) is defined over T*, so every variable must have been rewritten before the derivation stops.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parser generators such as yacc, bison and ANTLR read this grammar written in BNF or EBNF with declarations and actions, and build parse tables from it. Published standards for SQL, JSON and C state their grammar as normative text. Grammar-based fuzzing feeds random derivations into compilers to find crashes, and grammar inference tries to learn a grammar from example strings, still open research. Search for EBNF, ANTLR grammar file, or grammar-based fuzzing to go further.
